# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–20 (Complete – Updated 148)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of fifth year** (Chapter 20). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; collapses after heavy drinking, becomes helpless "whimpering old idiot," dies during summer. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies. Pitt comes to town in November to see lawyers, stays nearly a week in Curzon Street with Rawdon and Rebecca. **House renovation (November through Chapter 20)**: Determined upon Pitt's November arrival; Pitt's mansion in Great Gaunt Street undergoes extensive renovation—black brick coating removed revealing cheerful face streaked white, bronze knocker gilded, railings painted, becoming smartest house in quarter before green leaves replace yellow ones at Queen's Crawley. Work completed before winter; brothers' families agreed to meet at Christmas in country. **Christmas journey and arrival (Chapter 20)**: A day or two before Christmas, Becky, Rawdon, and little Rawdon travel to Queen's Crawley; little Rawdon rides on coach roof with father at White Horse Cellar at dawn; frost silvered hedges; road muddy with ruts and puddles after thaw; arrive at Mudbury in darkness; proceed to Hall with blazing windows and Christmas welcome. **Christmas Day gathering and aftermath (Chapter 20)**: All Crawleys from Rectory come to dine; Reverend Bute Crawley later joins Sir Huddlestone Fuddlestone's fox-hunt at half-past ten with Tom Moody's hounds, young gentlemen on thoroughbreds, Sir Huddlestone on clever cob. Little Rawdon remains on doorsteps after hunt departs, wondering and happy. Before Christmas ends, Pitt gives Rawdon second draft on bankers for hundred pounds, causing him "cruel pangs at first" but making him feel generous afterward. Rawdon and little Rawdon depart with "utmost heaviness of heart"; Rebecca and ladies part "with some alacrity." Rebecca returns to London to continue occupations; Great Gaunt Street house "quite rejuvenescent and ready for the reception of Sir Pitt and his family" when Baronet comes to London for Parliament duties.
- **Parliamentary activity (Chapter 20)**: Pitt attends first session as profound dissembler hiding projects; presents petition from Mudbury; attends assiduously in place and learns thoroughly House routine and business. At home peruses Blue Books to alarm and wonder of Lady Jane, who fears he kills himself by late hours. Makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs, determining to rank among them before many years pass.
- **Osborne household crisis (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: Old Mr. Osborne's financial collapse imminent. After Jane Osborne tells father she saw his grandson (George), he shows no anger but kindly voice; within fortnight, inquires of little French watch Jane used to wear (suggesting meditated response and Dobbin family inquiries). Mr. Osborne formally offers to take boy as heir to intended fortune, make allowance for Amelia, permit occasional visits only. **Amelia's refusal**: When letter delivered by Mr. Poe (attorney), Amelia trembles, flushes, tears letter into hundred fragments, declares "I marry again! I take money to part from my child!" Calls proposal cowardly; refuses answer; bows attorney out like tragedy Queen. **Sedley financial deterioration (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: Old Sedley dabbles in speculation despite Mr. Clapp's remonstrances; never tells how far engaged; wine and coal companies failed. Bills fall into arrear; remittances from India not arrived. Tradesmen angry at delay. First six months pass with Sedley keeping notion shares must rise. No sixty pounds arrives at half-year's end; household deepens into trouble. Mrs. Sedley grows infirm, weeps with Mrs. Clapp in kitchen. Butcher surly, grocer insolent; little Georgy grumbles about dinners. Amelia sacrifices private purse to keep son in health. **Amelia's sacrifice and Christmas gift (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: When own money received, Amelia proposes keeping portion for Georgy's new suit; Jos's remittances discovered not paid. Mother reveals house in difficulties Amelia should have seen; Amelia passes all money across table without word, returns to cry. Must countermand promised Christmas clothes; breaks matter to Georgy who makes loud outcry—"Everybody had new clothes at Christmas. The others would laugh at him." Amelia remembers India shawl Dobbin sent her; walks to Ludgate Hill India shop flushed and eager; merchant gives twenty guineas. Purchases Parents' Assistant and Sandford and Merton Georgy longed for; writes in fly-leaf "George Osborne, A Christmas gift from his affectionate mother." Books extant to this day with fair delicate superscription. Amelia's determination to provide despite financial ruin demonstrates maternal love against Osborne wealth coercion.
- **Locations**: (As before, plus) Brompton cottage, Ludgate Hill, Darton's shop St. Paul's Churchyard, Harrowgate.
- **Year 1818 (referenced)**: Miss Osborne receives drawing lessons from Mr. Smee, portrait-painter and R.A.

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Manipulation and cultivation of Pitt**: During November visit, Rebecca goes alone to greet Pitt at hotel, invites him to lodge at Curzon Street; her hospitalities irresistible through artless and frank warmth. She cooks salmi of Lord Steyne's pheasants, serves white wine from Marquis of Steyne's cellars (falsely claiming Rawdon picked it up cheaply from France), listens with "tenderest kindly interest" while hemming shirt for little Rawdon, sings and coaxes him. When departing, kisses hand from carriage, performance moves Pitt emotionally; he broods that she "respected him" and that Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" by comparison. Rebecca delicately hinted all these comparisons herself. **Financial manipulation**: Rebecca accepted small sum for little Rawdon's benefit via check from Pitt. **Authority over house renovation**: Given full orders by Pitt to sell, barter, confiscate, or purchase furniture; oversees Miss Briggs and little Rawdon in superintending female band stitching blinds and hangings.
- **Financial credit and Lord Steyne's carriage**: Sight of Marquis of Steyne's carriage-lamps at her door at midnight kept creditor faith; suggests creditors extend credit believing her to be Steyne's mistress. Rebecca described as "guiltless very likely" yet "writhing and pushing onward towards what they call 'a position in society.'"
- **Contempt for Lady Jane and psychological warfare**: Rebecca's profound dissembler; hides scorn for Lady Jane's "sweetness and kindness," finding her goodness "annoying." When Lady Jane tells stories to children clustered about her knees, Rebecca enters sneering with "green scornful eyes"; poor Lady Jane grows silent under "baleful glances"; her "simple little fancies shrank away tremulously, as fairies in the story-books, before a superior bad angel." Rebecca caricatures Court suit, shows sketch to Lord Steyne who carries it off delighted. Rebecca tells Steyne she has "no taste for bread and butter" when caricaturing Lady Jane. Rebecca and Lady Jane do not see much of each other except when younger brother's wife, having object to gain, frequents her; they "my-loved and my-deared each other assiduously, but kept apart generally."
- **Court presentation and Lord Steyne's patronage**: Lord Steyne met Pitt at Mrs. Becky's house, been gracious to new Baronet and member; impressed Pitt by deference shown to Rebecca, her ease and sprightliness in conversation, delight with which other men listened to her. Steyne made no doubt Pitt had only commenced career in public life; as neighbours, hoped when Lady Steyne arrived she would have honour of making acquaintance of Lady Crawley; left calling card within day or two, never having thought fit to notice predecessor though lived near century past.
- **Maternal rejection**: Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind at Christmas but for Lady Jane's urgent invitations and Rawdon's "symptoms of revolt and discontent" at her neglect of son.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Parliamentary ambition**: First session as profound dissembler hiding projects; presents petition from Mudbury only; attends assiduously, learns thoroughly House routine and business. At home peruses Blue Books to alarm of Lady Jane, who fears he kills himself by late hours. Makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs, determining to rank among them before many years pass. Displays complacency examining his thin Court suit legs, thinking himself "killing."
- **November visit and emotional response**: Comes to town November to see lawyers; lodges nearly week with Rawdon and Rebecca at Curzon Street. Appreciates Rebecca's salmi and wine from Steyne's cellars. Each day returns from Gray's Inn lawyers to Curzon Street's blazing fire with increasing gladness; feels "quite a pang at departing" when leaving. Broods that Rebecca respected him, that Rawdon is "foolish dull fellow," that Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" compared to "brilliant little Becky."
- **Financial circumstances and continued concealment**: Knows brother's family has nothing to live upon; aware he appropriated money that ought to have fallen to younger brother; feels "secret pangs of remorse." When Rebecca delicately obtained money for Rawdon's creditors, Pitt grew alarmed and launched long explanation of his own straitened circumstances: tenants won't pay, father's expenses involved him, wants to pay off incumbrances, bankers and agents overdrawn. Made compromise with Rebecca, giving small sum for little Rawdon's benefit. **Christmas generosity**: Before Christmas ends, screwed up courage to give brother another draft on bankers for hundred pounds—act causing him "cruel pangs at first" but making him "glow afterwards to think himself one of the most generous of men." Encourages Jim of Rectory to pay addresses to young lady with understanding he shall be presented to living when vacated.
- **At Christmas dinner**: Sits at head of table with Rebecca at right hand, uncommonly attentive to sister-in-law; perches Rawdon Junior on high chair by his side after dinner; reads prayers from great gilt book with domestics.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 20)**
- **Increasing isolation and subjugation**: In midst of Rebecca's intrigues, Rawdon feels himself more and more isolated every day. Allowed to go to club more; to dine abroad with bachelor friends; to come and go when liked, without questions asked. Sits for hours in brother's house very silent, thinking, doing little as possible. Glad to be employed on errand. "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission." Delilah (Rebecca) imprisoned him, cut his hair off. "Bold and reckless young blood of ten-years back was subjugated and was turned into a torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman."
- **Concern for son and family**: Strong attachment to little Rawdon; manifests "symptoms of revolt and discontent" at Rebecca's neglect of boy. Tells Rebecca reproachfully, "He's the finest boy in England... and you don't seem to care for him, Becky, as much as you do for your spaniel." **Christmas activities**: Wraps little Rawdon in shawls and comforters; hoists child onto roof of coach at White Horse Cellar; answers all boy's questions connected with road. Walks and rides with brother Pitt examining improvements, discussing estate matters. Departs with "utmost heaviness of heart" after Christmas.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Physical description**: Fine open-faced boy with blue eyes and waving flaxen hair; sturdy in limb; generous and soft in heart; about eight years old.
- **Christmas journey and activities**: Rides on coach roof with father at White Horse Cellar at dawn; journey "of infinite pleasure"; father answers all questions. At Hall, enters "perfect palace of enchantment and wonder" with galleries, ancient bedrooms, pictures, china, armour. Takes command of small party with Pitt Binkie and Matilda; they follow him with "great reverence"; his happiness and pleasure in country "extreme." Fox-hunt spectacle famous sight for little Rawdon; remains on doorsteps after hunt departs—"wondering and happy." Departs with "utmost heaviness of heart."

**Amelia Osborne (Mrs. George Osborne) (Chapter 20 – NEW)**
- **Refusal of Osborne's offer**: When Mr. Osborne formally offers to make little George heir to fortune and provide Amelia allowance, conditioned on child living entirely with grandfather with only occasional permitted visits, Amelia responds with rare anger. Tears letter into hundred fragments, declares "I marry again! I take money to part from my child! Who dares insult me by proposing such a thing?" Calls proposal cowardly; refuses answer; bows attorney (Mr. Poe) out like tragedy Queen.
- **Maternal sacrifice and Christmas determination**: As Sedley household falls into financial ruin, Amelia prioritizes son's welfare above all. Parents never remark her agitation over Osborne's letter; she never tells them of interview. When household finances collapse and promised Christmas clothes must be countermanded, Amelia breaks matter to Georgy who makes "loud outcry." Despite poverty, Amelia remembers India shawl sent by Dobbin; walks to Ludgate Hill India shop flushed and eager, sells shawl for twenty guineas; purchases parents' Assistant and Sandford and Merton Georgy longed for; writes in fly-leaf "George Osborne, A Christmas gift from his affectionate mother." Books extant to this day with fair delicate superscription. Amelia's devotion demonstrated through sacrifice despite financial ruin and Osborne coercion.

**Minor Characters (Chapter 20)**
- **Mr. Osborne**: Old gentleman; after Jane tells him she saw his grandson, shows no anger but kindly voice; within fortnight, meditated on matter and made inquiries of Dobbin family regarding her visit; formally offers to make George heir, provide Amelia allowance, permit occasional visits only; calls himself Mr. O. in letter.
- **Mr. Poe (attorney)**: Brings or reads Osborne's letter to Amelia; witnesses her rare anger; describes her tearing letter, calling proposal cowardly, bowing him out like tragedy Queen.
- **Old Mr. Sedley**: Dabbles in speculation despite Mr. Clapp's remonstrances; never dares tell how far engaged; wine and coal companies failed; bills fall into arrear; remittances from India not arrived; keeps notion shares must rise; never talks about money matters before women.
- **Mrs. Sedley**: Growing infirm and shaken; remains silent or weeps a great deal with Mrs. Clapp in kitchen.
- **Mr. Clapp**: Former servant of old Sedley; after master's disaster, found other employment quickly; remains faithfully attached despite falling off of wealthy friends; remonstrates against Sedley's speculations but Sedley never dares tell him extent of engagement.
- **Nynelle Hollmere** (formerly Thiena Hollwood): Resident of fragmentary Miremere/Gulton narrative; mended torn sleeve by window, said little; argued with carter over price of sack of oats; hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step; complained of aching back; narrative function remains unclear, isolated from main Crawley-Osborne plot.

## Critical Facts
- **Osborne's financial coercion and Amelia's maternal integrity**: Mr. Osborne attempts to purchase custody of little George through allowance conditioned on separation from mother. Amelia's refusal demonstrates maternal love transcends financial security; she prefers poverty with son to wealth obtained through separation.
- **Sedley family financial collapse imminent**: Bills in arrear; remittances from India not arrived; speculation failing; household approaching ruin. Amelia sacrifices personal needs (Christmas clothes for herself) to provide for little Georgy. Her sale of Dobbin's gift (India shawl) to purchase son's Christmas books demonstrates hierarchy of values: child's education and happiness surpass sentimental keepsakes.
- **Rebecca's psychological dominance continues**: Rebecca's campaign of contempt, mocking presence, and strategic sabotage of Lady Jane continues to threaten Pitt's marriage and household stability through deliberate psychological warfare masked by civility.
- **Rawdon's complete subjugation**: Rawdon transformed from "bold and reckless young blood" into "torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman" through Rebecca's control. His son remains primary emotional anchor.
- **Little Rawdon's resilience**: Despite maternal rejection, child bonds profoundly with father and finds "extreme" happiness in country; father's active inclusion and validation counter mother's neglect.
